```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)
options(scipen = 999)
```

### Introduction

In the class activity, you tested a school board member's claim using data from Montgomery County, Pa. — and found a model that didn't hold up. Now you'll run the same analysis using data from Montgomery County, Md. Your job is to evaluate whether the Maryland data tells a different story, and what that means for how you'd report on the claim.

### Loading the Data

```{r}
schools <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405_files/refs/heads/main/montgomery_md.csv")
```

### Task 1: Examine the Data First (2 points)

Before you plot anything, look at the data — you know why by now.

```{r}
summary(schools$`FARMS Pct`)
schools |> arrange(desc(`FARMS Pct`)) |> head(10)
```

Are there any data quality issues like the ones you found in the Pennsylvania data? How does the distribution of FARMS percentages compare between the two counties? Note anything that concerns you or gives you confidence in the data.

There do not seem to be any major problems with the Maryland data. The FARMS percentages range from 4% to 96%, with an average of 39.07% and a median of 32.5%. Broad Acres Elementary has the highest percentage at 96%. One thing I noticed is that even schools with high FARMS percentages have different math scores. This shows that having more students receiving free or reduced price meals does not automatically mean students will perform poorly on math tests. but the data do look reasonable, but comparing it with pennsylvania will help us understand the differences between the two counties.

### Task 2: Create a Scatterplot and Compare (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to create a scatterplot of FARMS percentage vs. math scores for Montgomery County, Md.

```{r}
schools |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `FARMS Pct`, y = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "FARMS Percentage", y = "% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations",
       title = "Math Scores vs. FARMS Percentage, Montgomery County MD")
```

Describe what you see. Then compare this scatterplot specifically to the Pennsylvania one: what differences do you notice in the direction, strength, and spread of the relationship? The two counties share a name and are both suburban — what might explain why they look so different?

the maryland scatterplot shows a clear negative relationship between FARMS percentages and math scores. As the percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price meals increased, the percentage of students meeting math expectations generally decreases.lookinf at it, the points follow a downward pattern, although there is still some variation between schools. Compared to Pennsylvania, the results are very different. pennsylavnia showed a much weaker relationship with a slightly positive trend, while maryland shows a stronger negative relationship. one possible reason for this difference is that the two counties may have different school populations, resources, and economic conditions. Even though they share the same county name, their schools may face different challenges.

### Task 3: Linear Regression Model (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to run a linear regression model predicting math scores from FARMS percentage.

```{r}
model <- lm(`% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` ~ `FARMS Pct`, data = schools)
summary(model)
```

Report the three key statistics: the p-value, the Adjusted R-squared, and the coefficient for FARMS Pct. Then interpret them together — not separately. What does the combination of these three numbers tell you about the relationship between poverty and math scores in Montgomery County, Md.? Is this model worth using? How does it compare to the Pennsylvania model?

the regression results show a strong negative relationship between FARMS percentages and math scores in moco , maryland The p value is less than 0.0000000000000002, which means the relationship is statistically significant. The adjusted r squared is 0.6734, which means that about 67.34% of the differences in math scores can be explained by FARMS percentages. The FARMS coefficient is -0.59511, that means that for every 1 percentage point increase in FARMS, math scores are expected to decrease by about 0.60 percentage points. all together, these results show that FARMS percentages are strongly related to math performance in Maryland. I think this model is worth using because it explains a large portion of the differences in math scores. Compared to Pennsylvania, Maryland has a much stronger relationship, while the Pennsylvania model showed a weak relationship that was not statistically significant.

### Task 4: Identifying Schools with the Biggest Residuals (6 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME values with the correct variable names to calculate predicted values, residuals, and absolute residuals for each school. Then arrange the schools in descending order of absolute residuals.

```{r}
schools <- schools |>
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model),
    residual = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` - predicted,
    abs_residual = abs(residual)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_residual))

head(schools |> select(1, `FARMS Pct`,
                       `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`,
                       predicted, residual), 10)
```

Identify the school with the largest positive residual (doing much better than the model predicts) and the school with the largest negative residual (doing much worse). For each school, find its zip code and look it up on [CensusReporter.org](https://censusreporter.org).

For each of the two schools, answer:
- What does the demographic and economic profile of the zip code look like?
- Does anything in that profile help explain why the school is over- or under-performing the model?
- What would your first reporting question be to the principal of that school?

Fox Chapel Elementary (ZIP Code 20876):
The ZIP code has a population of about 26,406 people. The median household income is $119,731, and about 9.8% of residents live below the poverty line. Around 52% of adults have a bachelor's degree or higher. About 35.7% of the population is foreign born. This shows that the area has people from different backgrounds and income levels. but, this does not fully explain why Fox Chapel performed so much better than the model predicted. My first question to the principal would be: What does the school do differently that helps students perform so well in math?

Germantown Elementary (ZIP Code 20874):
The ZIP code has a population of about 62,738 people. The median household income is $115,022, and about 8.3% of residents live below the poverty line. Around 48.9% of adults have a bachelor's degree or higher, and 37.1% of residents are foreign born. Even though the area has a fairly high household income, Germantown Elementary performed much worse than the model predicted. This makes me wonder if there are other problems within the school that could be affecting students' math scores. My first question to the principal would be: What challenges are students and teachers facing that could explain why the school's math scores are so much lower than expected?

### Task 5: Evaluate the Model and Write the Pitch (7 points)

You've now run this analysis on two counties. Return to the school board member's claim: that elementary schools with fewer students on free and reduced-price meals do better on standardized math tests.

Write a short story pitch of 4-6 sentences that addresses all of the following: Does the Maryland data support or contradict the claim? How does it compare to what you found in Pennsylvania? What would you ask the school board member if you called them for comment? And what's the most interesting specific finding from your residuals analysis: which school would you want to visit first, and why?

a closer look at elementary schools in MOCO, Maryland, shows that schools with more students receiving free or reduced price meals tend to have lower math scores. this supports the school board members claim, but the results are very different from Pennsylvania, where there was no strong relationship between FARMS percentages and math performance. I would want to ask the school board member if they have considered how school funding, resources, and extra academic support might also affect students' test scores. but, not every school followed this pattern. Fox Chapel Elementary stood out because its students scored almost 30 percentage points higher than the model predicted, even though more than half of its students receive free or reduced-price meals. I would want to visit Fox Chapel first to see what the school is doing differently and find out what other schools could learn from its success.
